anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level knobs (memory, checkpoint, log, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, causing avoidable pressure on subsystems even when raw resources are available.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical or virtual storage layer cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded by the database, resulting in persistently high I/O latency, deep device queues, and long database I/O waits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server transport, listener, or socket resources are saturated or unstable, producing connection errors, socket backlogs, and prolonged data-transfer waits.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set:  • Sudden surges in checkpoint, page-flush, or log-write waits elongate transaction commit paths while storage latency and queue depth remain elevated.  • Back-end workers stall on I/O, hold locks, and accumulate in client-write or client-read waits, inflating active session counts and exhausting connection slots.  • Application servers observe both slow statement execution and sporadic connection refusals; retry storms further inflate throughput demand, amplifying storage and CPU spikes that appear inconsistent with overall hardware utilization.  • Monitoring shows oscillating CPU usage (from spin waits on mis-set parameters) co-occurring with storage wait domination and rising TCP retransmissions or listener backlog overflows, making single-layer diagnosis misleading.

Causal chain: Sub-optimal configuration parameters—such as an undersized buffer pool or overly aggressive checkpoint interval—drive excessive physical I/O, pushing the storage subsystem to (or beyond) its throughput limits. The resulting I/O stalls propagate back into the engine, holding back-end processes longer and inflating connection lifetimes. As active back-ends linger, listener and socket resources saturate, and network round-trip delays grow; this, in turn, slows client consumption of result sets, prolonging hold times on server buffers and causing even more dirty pages to accumulate. The feedback loop between misconfiguration-induced I/O amplification, storage saturation, and network congestion reinforces each anomaly, degrading overall throughput and making the database appear resource-starved across multiple layers simultaneously.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
